text: Standard sign-in flows have a quiet problem for zero trust. A user signs in once, Entra ID issues an access token, and client applications present that token on every call afterward without signing in again. Convenient, but the token is normally honored for its entire lifetime, commonly around an hour, no matter what happens to the account in the meantime. This lesson is about the mechanism that closes that gap: Continuous Access Evaluation.

Picture the real incident scenario: an admin spots a compromised account in the sign-in logs and disables it at nine-oh-five. Without anything else in place, that doesn't matter to a token the attacker already holds — the resource provider has no way to know the account status changed, and keeps honoring that token until it naturally expires. Verification that only happens at token-issuance time is a snapshot, not continuous, and a zero-trust design built on verify-explicitly can't tolerate that gap.

Continuous Access Evaluation creates a near-real-time channel between Entra ID and supported resource providers — Microsoft Graph, Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams — so a defined set of critical events gets pushed and acted on within minutes instead of waiting out the token. Those events are: the account is disabled or deleted, the password is changed or reset, an admin explicitly revokes refresh tokens, or Identity Protection evaluates the user's risk as high. Microsoft has also extended this toward location-aware enforcement, re-checking Conditional Access location policies mid-session rather than only at the next refresh.

This is the piece that makes continuous verification literally true. A login-time check answers whether a request was trustworthy when it was made. CAE answers whether the session is still trustworthy right now — a different question, because a session legitimate at nine a-m can become illegitimate minutes later if the account is compromised, disabled, or flagged high-risk in between. Both questions need answering in a real zero-trust architecture.

It also changes how you think about token lifetime as a control. Without CAE, shortening token lifetime is one of the few levers you have to limit damage after a compromise, at the cost of more re-authentication and worse user experience. With CAE, a resource provider can hold a longer token with confidence, because revocation no longer depends on that token expiring — it depends on Entra ID pushing the signal the moment it has one. Next lesson adds the device itself as another signal in that same decision.
